title: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the role and impact of technology in society

lessons.title: What technology is and how it changed farming
lessons.html:
Technology solves problems

Technology is the use of knowledge, tools and materials to solve problems and meet people's needs. Technology is not only computers. A hoe, a plough, a windmill, a dip tank and a cellphone are all technology.

From hand tools to machines

ThenNow
Hand hoe and digging stickTractor with plough or planter
Oxen pulling a ploughDiesel tractors, some with GPS steering
Carrying water in bucketsPumps, pipes, drip and centre-pivot irrigation
Windmill on a boreholeSolar-powered pump
Writing records in a bookPhone apps and computers
Selling at the local market onlyCold chain and exports to other countries

Technology in daily life

Technology is everywhere around us: electricity, taxis and trucks, cellphones and WhatsApp, radio, clinics with medicines, and banking on a phone. Many farm workers now get paid into a bank account and can check their balance on a cellphone.

The design process

People make technology by following steps:

  1. Identify the problem, for example chickens getting wet in the rain.
  2. Investigate what has been tried before and what materials are available.
  3. Design ideas and choose the best one, such as a raised shelter with a sloping roof.
  4. Make it with suitable tools and materials.
  5. Evaluate: does it work? What can be improved?

Anyone can use this process to solve problems at home or at work.

Think of a dip tank on a cattle farm. The problem was ticks that spread disease. People investigated, designed a long, narrow concrete bath that animals swim through, built it, and then checked if tick numbers dropped. That is the design process in action.

lessons.title: Good and bad effects of technology
lessons.html:
Thinking critically

To think critically means to look at both sides before you decide something is good or bad. Technology brings benefits, but it can also cause problems.

Benefits

  • More food: better seed, fertiliser and irrigation give higher yields.
  • Less hard work: machines do heavy lifting and digging.
  • Health: vaccines for people and animals, clean water and medicines.
  • Communication: cellphones let farmers get weather warnings and market prices.
  • Safety: guards on machines, protective clothing and fire-fighting equipment.

Problems

  • Jobs: one machine can do the work of many people, so some jobs are lost. New jobs need new skills, for example operating or repairing machines.
  • Environment: chemicals can pollute rivers; diesel engines cause air pollution; plastic waste builds up.
  • Cost: new technology is expensive. Small farmers may not afford it, so the gap between rich and poor can grow.
  • Dependence: when the power goes off during load shedding, electric pumps and cold rooms stop.
  • Safety risks: machines can injure people who are not trained.
  • Privacy and scams: cellphones bring fraud messages that try to steal money.

Indigenous technology

Communities in South Africa have long used their own technology: clay pots that keep water cool, grain stores raised off the ground, kraals made from thorn branches, and knowledge of medicinal plants. These are still useful and often cheap and sustainable.

Making good choices

Before choosing a technology, ask: Does it solve the real problem? Can we afford it and maintain it? Is it safe? What will it do to people's jobs and to the environment?

Key points

  • Technology is using knowledge, tools and materials to solve problems.
  • The design process is identify, investigate, design, make and evaluate.
  • Technology can bring more food, less hard work and better health.
  • It can also cost jobs, pollute and widen the gap between rich and poor.
  • Think critically about benefits and problems before choosing a technology.
